en.title: Food Science and Technology: the whole course
en.short: What food science and technology is, how the degree is organised, the main areas, and how to study it.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Food Science and Technology studies food as a biological, chemical and physical material, and the systems that turn raw produce into safe, nutritious, acceptable and stable foods. Food science asks why food behaves as it does: how water, carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, minerals and enzymes react; how micro-organisms grow or are stopped; how heat, cold, drying and packaging change quality.

Food technology applies that knowledge in processing, preservation, product development, quality assurance and plant operation. The subject follows the food chain from farm and harvest through storage, processing, distribution, retail and consumption to waste and by-products. It is practical and evidence-based: claims about safety, shelf life or nutrition must be measured and documented.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Awards and lengths differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, a BSc or BTech in Food Science and Technology is commonly four to five years depending on the institution; polytechnics award the ND and HND under the National Board for Technical Education, and universities follow National Universities Commission benchmarks. Many programmes include an industrial attachment, often under SIWES.

In the United Kingdom, a BSc is commonly three years and a taught MSc one year. A master’s is usually one to two years depending on country and mode, and a PhD longer. The first year builds science foundations; middle years add food-specific core; the final year often has a project or dissertation. Some institutions name the degree Food Science, Food Technology or Food Science and Technology.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Teaching usually starts with foundations: the scope of the field and the food chain; food chemistry, beginning with water and carbohydrates, then proteins and lipids, then vitamins, minerals, enzymes and colour; food microbiology, including growth, injury and control; food-borne disease and hygiene; food composition and nutrition; mathematics and statistics; and food analysis and quality measurement. These give the language and laboratory habits for later work.

Core studies then move through food engineering, especially heat and mass transfer; rheology and texture; thermal processing such as blanching, pasteurisation and sterilisation; non-thermal and emerging methods; preservation principles and hurdle technology; packaging, including materials, migration and shelf life; and fermentation with starter cultures. Commodity technology follows: cereals, legumes and oilseeds; fruits, vegetables, roots and tubers; meat, fish, eggs and dairy; sugar, confectionery, beverages and convenience foods. Product development and sensory evaluation connect these to consumers.

The management and professional strand covers quality assurance, HACCP and food safety management, food laws, standards and labelling, risk assessment and emerging hazards, plant design, utilities and sanitation, waste, by-products and sustainability, economics, marketing and entrepreneurship, professional ethics and regulatory practice, and research methods leading to the final project. Master’s level revisits the science more deeply: advanced food chemistry and interfaces, advanced food microbiology and predictive risk modelling, advanced process engineering and novel technologies, and frontiers of the field with a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study food science as a chain of cause and effect. For each process, ask what is being controlled, by which variable, and how you would measure the result. Learn the chemistry and microbiology behind a number before memorising the number. In calculations, write the units at every step and check that the answer is physically sensible.

In the laboratory, record raw data, conditions and deviations; a result you cannot trace is not evidence. Read labels and standards from your own country and compare them with Codex texts, noting the source and date. Use spreadsheets for data and learn basic statistics. Revise by explaining a process aloud, then by solving a numerical problem without notes. Keep a glossary of terms such as water activity, D-value, z-value, hurdle and shelf life.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Common mistakes include treating food science as cookery; confusing food quality with food safety; and assuming a process is safe because it is traditional. Students mix up water activity with moisture content, sterilisation with pasteurisation, and shelf life with expiry date. They report a mean without variation, or a correlation as proof of cause.

In HACCP, they list hazards without linking them to control measures and critical limits. In labelling and law, they quote another country’s rule as universal. In projects, they choose a topic too broad, fail to define methods, or copy references without reading them. Check every figure against a current official source.

keyPoints: Food science explains why food behaves as it does; food technology applies that explanation to processing, preservation and products.
Safety and quality must be measured and documented, not assumed from tradition.
Water activity, pH, temperature, time and packaging are common controls in food preservation.
Thermal and non-thermal processes each have limits, and hurdle technology combines controls.
HACCP links hazards to control measures and critical limits; it is not just a list of hazards.
Check every law, standard, figure and shelf life claim against the current official source for the country concerned.

en.title: Food Science and Technology: Scope and the Food Chain
en.short: What food science, technology and engineering are, and where losses and hazards enter the food chain.

sections.heading: Three related fields
sections.text:
Food science is the scientific study of food: its composition, properties, reactions, microbiology, safety and behaviour from harvest to eating. Food technology is the practical use of that knowledge to turn raw materials into safe, stable, acceptable foods. It covers processing, preservation, packaging, storage and distribution. Food engineering applies engineering principles, such as heat, mass and momentum transfer, to design and control food processes and equipment.

The fields overlap. A food scientist may ask why a sauce separates. A food technologist decides how to stop it separating on the shelf. A food engineer sizes the mixer and heat exchanger. Food science explains, technology applies, engineering designs and scales.

sections.heading: The food chain
sections.text:
Food moves along a chain. It starts with farm inputs: seed, water, fertiliser, feed and labour. Production and harvest follow. Postharvest handling includes cleaning, sorting, drying, cooling and storage. Processing changes raw material into flour, oil, pasteurised milk or a ready meal. Distribution covers transport, wholesale, retail and cold chains (refrigerated handling). Consumption ends with preparation and eating.

Each link adds value but also risk.

sections.heading: Losses and hazards
sections.text:
Losses enter at every stage. In many lower-income countries, much loss occurs after harvest through spoilage, pests, poor drying, lack of cold storage and rough handling. In higher-income settings, more waste occurs at retail and household level. Safety hazards also enter early: soil and water can carry microbes, moulds can form toxins, and pesticide or veterinary drug residues may remain. Processing can introduce metal, allergens or unsafe additives if controls fail. Distribution can break the cold chain, and consumers can cross-contaminate food at home.

Controls include good hygiene, correct drying and cooling, safe packaging, traceability and separation of raw and cooked food.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: A small case: Amina grows tomatoes near Kano. She harvests in the heat, packs them in sacks and sends them by open truck. Bruising, heat and delay cause spoilage before market. Cooling, shallow crates and a shorter route would cut loss and microbial growth.

keyPoints: Food science studies food composition, properties, reactions, microbiology and safety.
Food technology applies food science to processing, preservation, packaging, storage and distribution.
Food engineering designs and controls food processes and equipment using engineering principles.
The food chain runs from farm inputs and harvest through postharvest handling, processing, distribution and consumption.
Losses occur after harvest through spoilage, pests, poor drying and weak cold chains, and later as retail and household waste.
Biological, chemical and physical hazards can enter at any link, so controls are needed from farm to fork.

en.title: Food Chemistry: Water Activity and Carbohydrates
en.short: Covers water activity, moisture, water states, sugars, starch changes and dietary fibre.

sections.heading: Water content and activity
sections.text:
Moisture content is the mass of water in food. Water activity (a_w) measures water available for reactions and microbes. It equals the equilibrium vapour pressure of water in the food divided by that of pure water at the same temperature, a_w = p/p0. Most bacteria need a_w above about 0.90; many yeasts and moulds grow lower.

Water is free or bound; the first, most tightly bound layer is called the monolayer. Free water is solvent and supports growth. Bound water is attached to solutes and surfaces. Drying, salting or adding sugar lowers a_w and extends shelf life. Moisture content alone does not predict stability.

sections.heading: Sugars and fibre
sections.text: Carbohydrates are classified by size. Monosaccharides are single units, such as glucose and fructose. Disaccharides are two units: sucrose, lactose and maltose. Oligosaccharides have a few units. Polysaccharides are long chains: starch, glycogen and cellulose. Reducing sugars can reduce mild oxidising agents; sucrose is non-reducing. Dietary fibre is carbohydrate that human enzymes cannot digest, including cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin and resistant starch. Soluble fibre forms gels; insoluble fibre adds bulk.

sections.heading: Starch changes
sections.text: Starch is stored as granules of amylose and amylopectin. Gelatinisation happens when starch is heated with enough water: granules absorb water, swell and burst, amylose leaks out, and viscosity rises. On cooling, a gel may form. This thickens sauces and sets puddings. Retrogradation is the reordering of gelatinised starch on cooling or storage. Amylose reassociates quickly and amylopectin crystallises more slowly; this makes bread firm and causes syneresis (liquid weeping). Dextrinisation is breakdown of starch by dry heat into shorter dextrins. It gives toast and crusts colour and flavour and reduces thickening power.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Suppose the equilibrium vapour pressure over a food is 1.8 kPa and that of pure water at the same temperature is 3.0 kPa. Then a_w = 1.8 ÷ 3.0 = 0.60. At this low activity most microorganisms cannot grow, so shelf life is long if packaging stops moisture pickup. If a_w rises to 0.85, many moulds and some yeasts can grow. Check a_w with a calibrated meter; limits vary.

keyPoints: Moisture content measures total water; water activity measures available water.
a_w = p/p0, where p is the equilibrium vapour pressure over the food and p0 is that of pure water at the same temperature.
Most bacteria need a_w above about 0.90; moulds and yeasts often grow at lower values.
Carbohydrates range from monosaccharides to polysaccharides; dietary fibre is non-digestible carbohydrate.
Gelatinisation thickens starch with heat and water; retrogradation firms gels and stales bread.
Dextrinisation is dry-heat breakdown of starch into dextrins, giving colour and flavour.

en.title: Food Chemistry: Proteins and Lipids
en.short: Amino acids, protein structure and function, fatty acids, triacylglycerols and rancidity.

sections.heading: Amino acids and structure
sections.text: Proteins are polymers of amino acids. Each amino acid has an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and a side chain (R group) on the same carbon. The side chain decides whether it is acidic, basic, polar or nonpolar. Amino acids join by peptide bonds into peptides and polypeptides. Protein structure has four levels: primary (amino acid sequence), secondary (local coils and sheets), tertiary (whole-chain 3D shape) and quaternary (several chains). Shape depends on weak bonds and disulfide links.

sections.heading: Denaturation and function
sections.text: Heat, acid, salt or beating can denature a protein: its folded shape unfolds, usually without breaking peptide bonds. This changes function. In gelation, proteins join into a network that traps water, as in set yoghurt or tofu. In emulsification, proteins and other emulsifiers such as lecithin coat oil droplets and stop them merging, as in mayonnaise. In foaming, proteins stabilise air bubbles, as in whisked egg white. Overbeating can damage the foam.

sections.heading: Fatty acids and lipids
sections.text: Fatty acids are chains with a carboxyl group. Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds and are usually solid; monounsaturated have one; polyunsaturated have two or more. Double bonds create cis or trans shapes: cis chains bend, trans chains stay straighter. A triacylglycerol (triglyceride) is glycerol joined by ester bonds to three fatty acids. Fats are solid triacylglycerols rich in saturated acids; oils are liquid and richer in unsaturated acids.

sections.heading: Rancidity
sections.text: Lipid oxidation is reaction with oxygen, often at double bonds, giving hydroperoxides that break down to aldehydes and ketones with stale or painty smells. Light, heat and metals speed it. Hydrolysis splits ester bonds, releasing free fatty acids; in butter this gives a soapy or rancid taste. Example: cooking oil left open in sunlight oxidises faster than oil stored closed in a dark cupboard. Antioxidants and low oxygen slow oxidation.

keyPoints: Amino acids join by peptide bonds, and their side chains determine protein properties.
Protein structure has primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary levels.
Denaturation unfolds a protein without usually breaking peptide bonds and changes its functional properties.
Gelation traps water, emulsification stabilises oil droplets, and foaming stabilises air bubbles.
Triacylglycerols are glycerol esters of three fatty acids, and saturation affects melting point.
Rancidity comes from lipid oxidation or hydrolysis and is slowed by antioxidants, low oxygen, and control of heat and light.

en.title: Food Chemistry: Vitamins, Minerals, Enzymes and Colour
en.short: Vitamins and minerals by function, enzyme kinetics and inhibition, and food pigments.

sections.heading: Vitamins and minerals
sections.text:
Vitamins and minerals are micronutrients. Vitamins are grouped by solubility and function. Water-soluble vitamins (B group and C) mostly act as coenzymes; vitamin C is also an antioxidant. Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K cover vision, calcium regulation, antioxidant defence and blood clotting. Minerals include electrolytes (sodium, potassium, chloride), bone minerals (calcium, phosphorus, magnesium), enzyme cofactors (zinc, copper, selenium) and iron for oxygen transport.

Processing and storage reduce them differently. Water-soluble vitamins leach into cooking water and are destroyed by heat, light and oxygen. Fat-soluble vitamins oxidise with light, heat and oxygen. Minerals are not destroyed by heat but leach into water. Losses vary with food and conditions, so check current food composition tables.

sections.heading: Enzymes in food
sections.text:
Enzymes are proteins that catalyse reactions by lowering activation energy. For a simple enzyme, v = Vmax × [S] ÷ (Km + [S]). Vmax is the maximum rate; Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax, so a low Km means high affinity. Worked example: if Vmax = 10 units and Km = 5 mM, at [S] = 5 mM, v = 10 × 5 ÷ (5 + 5) = 5 units.

Inhibitors slow enzymes. A competitive inhibitor binds the active site and raises apparent Km; a noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and lowers Vmax. Polyphenol oxidase causes browning and lipase causes rancidity. Heat and pH extremes inactivate enzymes, and low water slows them; blanching uses heat deliberately.

sections.heading: Colour pigments
sections.text:
Natural pigments give colour directly. Chlorophyll is green; carotenoids give yellow, orange and red; anthocyanins give red, blue and purple and change with pH; betalains occur in beetroot; myoglobin gives red meat its colour. Reaction-based colours form during processing. Maillard browning occurs when sugars and amino groups react under heat; caramelisation is sugar breakdown by heat; enzymatic browning is polyphenol oxidase acting on phenols when plant cells are damaged.

Processing changes colour. Heat turns chlorophyll olive-brown, anthocyanins are heat and light sensitive, and carotenoids oxidise. These changes affect appearance.

keyPoints: Vitamins are grouped by solubility and function; water-soluble vitamins act mainly as coenzymes.
Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K can oxidise with light, heat and oxygen.
Minerals are not destroyed by heat but can leach into cooking water.
Michaelis-Menten: v = Vmax × [S] ÷ (Km + [S]); Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax.
Competitive inhibition raises apparent Km; noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax.
Natural pigments include chlorophyll, carotenoids, anthocyanins, betalains and myoglobin; Maillard, caramelisation and enzymatic browning are reaction-based colours.

en.title: Food Microbiology: Growth, Injury and Control
en.short: How bacteria, yeasts and moulds grow in food, why viruses and parasites do not, and what each control factor achieves.

sections.heading: Contaminant groups
sections.text: Bacteria are single cells dividing by binary fission; they grow fastest and some form heat-resistant spores. Yeasts are single-celled fungi that bud, tolerate acid and sugar, and spoil food by making gas and alcohol. Moulds are filamentous fungi that grow at lower water activity and may produce mycotoxins (fungal poisons such as aflatoxin). Viruses and parasites cannot multiply in food, only in a living host, so their numbers do not rise; norovirus and hepatitis A are the main food-borne viruses.

sections.heading: The growth curve
sections.text:
In food, bacteria pass through lag, exponential, stationary and death phases. In lag, cells adapt and injured cells repair, so numbers stay flat. In exponential phase cells divide at a constant interval, the generation time. Stationary phase begins when nutrients run out or waste builds up; death follows.

Example: 100 cells, generation time 30 minutes. Reaching 10⁶ needs 10⁶ ÷ 10² = 10⁴, about 13.3 doublings; 13.3 × 30 = 400 minutes, about 6.6 hours.

sections.heading: Growth factors and control
sections.text:
Growth depends on water activity (aw, water available for use), pH, temperature, oxygen and nutrients. Most bacteria need aw above about 0.91 and pH near neutral; yeasts and moulds tolerate acid and lower aw, some moulds near 0.80. Psychrotrophs grow when chilled, mesophiles in the middle, thermophiles when hot. Aerobes need oxygen, anaerobes are inhibited by it, facultative organisms use either.

Each control targets one of these factors or the cells themselves: drying and salting lower aw, acid lowers pH, chilling slows growth, modified atmosphere removes oxygen, preservatives inhibit or damage cells.

sections.heading: Spores, biofilms, injury
sections.text:
Spores are dormant, tough-walled forms of Bacillus, Clostridium and some moulds. They resist heat, drying and chemicals, survive pasteurisation, and germinate when conditions improve; killing them needs far more heat, such as 121 °C.

Biofilms are cells attached to a surface in a slime of extracellular polymers; they resist rinsing and disinfectants, so clean mechanically first.

Injured cells are sublethally damaged by heat, acid or cold. They may not grow on selective media yet can repair and grow later, so a negative test can understate risk.

keyPoints: Bacteria grow fastest in food; yeasts and moulds tolerate more acid and less water, while viruses and parasites do not multiply in food at all.
The growth curve has lag, exponential, stationary and death phases; the generation time sets how fast numbers rise in exponential phase.
Water activity, pH, temperature, oxygen and nutrients each limit growth, and each control measure works by changing one of them or by inhibiting the cells.
Bacterial spores survive pasteurisation and need much higher heat to kill.
Biofilms resist disinfectants, so surfaces must be cleaned mechanically first.
Injured cells may be missed by tests but can repair and grow, so a negative result does not prove safety.

en.title: Food-borne Disease and Hygiene Practice
en.short: Food infection, intoxication and toxin-mediated infection, plus hygiene and pest control in a food plant.

sections.heading: Three types
sections.text: Food-borne illness is any illness caused by food. A food infection happens when live organisms are swallowed and then grow or invade the body; symptoms appear after an incubation period. A food intoxication happens when a toxin is already in the food before eating, so the organism may be dead. A toxin-mediated infection happens when organisms are swallowed, grow in the gut, and make toxin there. Ask where the toxin was made.

sections.heading: Organisms and syndromes
sections.text: Staphylococcus aureus causes intoxication: vomiting and cramps within 1 to 6 hours, and its toxin survives reheating. Clostridium botulinum causes botulism, a descending paralysis with double vision and breathing difficulty; the neurotoxin is preformed, often in improperly canned low-acid food. Bacillus cereus has an emetic toxin (vomiting, 1 to 6 hours) and a diarrhoeal toxin made in the gut. Salmonella causes infection with diarrhoea, fever and cramps. Listeria monocytogenes causes listeriosis, which is severe in pregnant women and people with weak immunity. E. coli O157:H7 causes bloody diarrhoea and haemolytic uraemic syndrome, a serious kidney and blood disorder. Clostridium perfringens causes toxin-mediated diarrhoea and cramps. Vibrio cholerae causes profuse watery diarrhoea and dehydration.

sections.heading: Hygiene in the plant
sections.text: Personal hygiene means clean hands, clean protective clothing, no jewellery, covered cuts and exclusion of ill workers. Cleaning removes food soil and grease; sanitation then reduces microorganisms to a safe level. Clean before sanitising, because soil shields microbes. Pest control denies pests food, water and shelter through proofing, screens, seals, waste removal, inspection and traps. These practices break the chain from hands, equipment, pests and raw food to the product.

sections.heading: Case in Ibadan
sections.text: At a small plant in Ibadan, a worker with a septic finger handled cooked rice that was held warm for hours. Staphylococcus aureus grew and made enterotoxin. Reheating killed the bacteria but not the toxin. Students who ate the rice vomited two to four hours later. The fix is to exclude infected workers, cover wounds and cool food quickly.

keyPoints: A food infection comes from live organisms; a food intoxication comes from toxin already in the food; a toxin-mediated infection comes from toxin made in the gut.
Staphylococcus aureus and Clostridium botulinum cause intoxication, Salmonella and Listeria cause infection, and Clostridium perfringens causes toxin-mediated infection.
Handwashing, clean clothing, covering cuts and excluding ill workers reduce contamination from people.
Clean first, then sanitise, because food soil protects microorganisms from the sanitiser.
Pest control denies pests food, water and shelter, and so stops them carrying pathogens to food.
In the Ibadan rice case, reheating did not destroy staphylococcal toxin, so worker exclusion and rapid cooling were needed.

en.title: Food Composition and Human Nutrition
en.short: Proximate composition, Atwater energy calculation, nutrient needs, protein quality and dietary assessment.

sections.heading: Proximate composition
sections.text: Proximate analysis groups a food into moisture, ash (minerals), crude protein, crude fat, crude fibre and nitrogen-free extract (NFE). Protein is estimated from nitrogen, usually nitrogen × 6.25. NFE is carbohydrate by difference, not a direct measurement. These fractions are useful but crude: ash is not a full mineral profile, and crude fibre is not all dietary fibre.

sections.heading: Energy calculation
sections.text:
Energy is calculated by multiplying grams of energy-yielding components by Atwater factors. General factors are protein 4 kcal/g, fat 9 kcal/g and carbohydrate 4 kcal/g; alcohol gives 7 kcal/g. Fibre may be counted at 2 kcal/g in some systems, or excluded. Specific factors exist for particular foods, so check the official table used in your country.

Worked example: 100 g of a food contains 10 g protein, 5 g fat, 20 g available carbohydrate and 2 g fibre.
Protein: 10 × 4 = 40 kcal
Fat: 5 × 9 = 45 kcal
Carbohydrate: 20 × 4 = 80 kcal
Fibre: 2 × 2 = 4 kcal
Total = 40 + 45 + 80 + 4 = 169 kcal per 100 g.

sections.heading: Nutrient needs and protein quality
sections.text:
Macronutrients supply energy and building material. Adult protein needs are often about 0.8 g per kg body weight per day; fat and carbohydrate recommendations are given as ranges of energy intake. Requirements vary with age, sex, activity, pregnancy and illness, so use current WHO, FAO or national tables. Micronutrients are vitamins and minerals needed in small amounts; they do not supply energy but support metabolism. Deficiencies and excesses both matter.

Protein quality depends on essential amino acid pattern and digestibility. PDCAAS (Protein Digestibility Corrected Amino Acid Score) = amino acid score × faecal digestibility, capped at 1.00. The amino acid score compares the limiting amino acid in the test protein with the same amino acid in a reference pattern. DIAAS (Digestible Indispensable Amino Acid Score) is a newer ileal digestibility measure.

sections.heading: Dietary assessment
sections.text: Dietary assessment estimates usual intake. Common methods are 24-hour recall, food frequency questionnaire, weighed food record and duplicate diet. Each has error: recall depends on memory, records can change behaviour, and tables have limited foods. Compare intake with requirements and interpret with caution. A single day does not show usual intake.

keyPoints: Proximate composition reports moisture, ash, crude protein, crude fat, crude fibre and nitrogen-free extract.
Protein is usually calculated as nitrogen × 6.25.
Atwater general factors: protein 4, fat 9, carbohydrate 4 kcal/g; alcohol 7 kcal/g.
PDCAAS = amino acid score × faecal digestibility, capped at 1.00.
Nutrient requirements vary by person and country; use current official tables.
Dietary assessment methods have errors; compare usual intake, not one day, with requirements.

en.title: Mathematics and Statistics for Food Science
en.short: This summary covers units, logs, calculus, statistics, regression and experimental design for food data.

sections.heading: Units and logs
sections.text:
Keep units consistent. Convert to SI: 1 g = 1000 mg, 1 kJ = 1000 J, 1 Pa = 1 N/m². Check dimensions: q = kA ΔT/L gives watts only with k in W/(m·K), A in m², ΔT in K, L in m.

Rearranging algebra: from N = N0 e^(−kt), take natural logs, ln(N/N0) = −kt, so k = −ln(N/N0)/t. Base-10 logs give log reduction: log(N0/N) = kt/2.303.

sections.heading: Rates and calculus
sections.text:
A derivative is a rate. First-order death, dN/dt = −kN, integrates to N = N0 e^(−kt). Fourier’s law q = −kA dT/dx and Fick’s law J = −D dC/dx describe heat and mass transfer. Integration adds accumulation or area under a curve.

Worked example: N0 = 1,000,000, k = 0.20 per minute, t = 10 min. N = 1,000,000 × e^(−2) = 135,335, about 1.4 × 10^5. Log reduction = 2 ÷ 2.303 = 0.87.

sections.heading: Statistics and tests
sections.text:
Descriptive statistics: mean, standard deviation (SD, spread), standard error (SE = SD/√n, precision of mean) and coefficient of variation (CV = SD/mean × 100%). In a normal distribution about 68% of values lie within mean ± 1 SD and 95% within ± 2 SD.

A 95% confidence interval is mean ± t(s/√n); t is about 1.96 for large n. A hypothesis test compares a null hypothesis with data; p is the probability of results at least this extreme if the null is true. p < 0.05 is common but arbitrary. Regression fits y = a + bx; R² is the share of variation explained. Correlation is not causation.

sections.heading: Design and labels
sections.text: Design of experiments varies factors at set levels with replication, randomisation and blocking, so effects are not confounded; factorial designs test factors together. On a food label, read the basis (per 100 g or per serving) and units. An assay result should state mean ± SD, n and method. Report significant figures honestly: 12.3 ± 0.2 g/100 g, not 12.34567.

keyPoints: Convert all quantities to consistent SI units and check dimensions before calculating.
First-order microbial death follows N = N0 e^(−kt), so ln(N/N0) = −kt.
Fourier’s law q = −kA dT/dx and Fick’s law J = −D dC/dx link gradients to heat and mass transfer rates.
Standard error is SE = SD/√n, and a 95% confidence interval is mean ± t(s/√n).
A hypothesis test reports p, the probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis is true.
Regression fits y = a + bx; R² measures explained variation, not causation.

en.title: Food Analysis and Quality Measurement
en.short: Sampling, calibration, wet and instrumental tests, and sensory panels as measuring tools.

sections.heading: Sampling and calibration
sections.text:
Analysis begins with a representative sample: a portion that has the same composition as the bulk lot. A sampling plan states how many increments to take, from where and how to combine them. Reduce bulk samples by quartering, grind and mix, and store so composition does not change. Sample preparation must not add or remove water, fat or volatiles.

Calibration compares an instrument response with known standards, such as buffer solutions for pH or certified reference materials. A blank and replicates are run. Figures of merit describe the method: accuracy (closeness to the true value), precision (agreement between repeats), sensitivity (response per unit concentration), limit of detection, linear range, selectivity and robustness.

sections.heading: Wet chemical methods
sections.text:
Moisture is usually found by oven drying, but volatile substances can be lost. Fat is extracted with a solvent such as petroleum ether in a Soxhlet apparatus. Protein is measured by Kjeldahl: digest with acid, distil ammonia, titrate, then multiply nitrogen by a factor, often 6.25. Ash is the residue after incineration in a muffle furnace. pH uses a glass electrode calibrated with buffers. Titratable acidity measures total acid by titration with standard alkali.

Example: 10.0 mL juice needs 8.5 mL of 0.100 M NaOH. For citric acid, equivalent weight E = 64.04 g/eq.
% acid (w/v) = (V × M × E × 100) ÷ (1000 × V_sample)
= (8.5 × 0.100 × 64.04 × 100) ÷ (1000 × 10.0) = 0.544% w/v.

sections.heading: Instruments and sensory panels
sections.text:
Colour is measured with a colorimeter or spectrophotometer, often as L*a*b* values: lightness and two colour axes. Texture is measured with a texture analyser that compresses, punctures or cuts a sample and records force and distance. These instruments give repeatable numbers but do not measure liking.

A sensory panel is a measuring instrument made of people. Panellists need clear definitions, training, controlled samples and replication. A trained panel can score intensity; a consumer panel measures preference. Panels are used where no instrument captures human perception, and they must be checked for agreement.

keyPoints: Take a representative sample and prepare it without changing composition.
Calibrate instruments with standards and run blanks and replicates.
Accuracy is closeness to truth; precision is agreement between repeats.
Kjeldahl nitrogen × 6.25 estimates protein; Soxhlet estimates fat.
Titratable acidity: % acid = (V × M × E × 100) ÷ (1000 × V_sample).
Sensory panels are instruments: train, control and replicate them.

en.title: Food Engineering: Heat and Mass Transfer
en.short: Material and energy balances, fluid flow, heat transfer, thermal and refrigeration calculations, drying and evaporation.

sections.heading: Balances and flow
sections.text: An engineering calculation starts with a material balance: mass in equals mass out plus accumulation. At steady state accumulation is zero. An energy balance does the same for enthalpy: energy in equals energy out plus accumulation. Fluid flow is described by flow rate, velocity and pressure. The continuity equation says mass flow rate is density times area times velocity. Pressure falls along a pipe because of friction, and pumps supply energy to overcome it.

sections.heading: Heat transfer modes
sections.text: Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation. Conduction is transfer through a stationary material, given by Fourier’s law: Q/t = kAΔT/L, where k is thermal conductivity, A area, ΔT temperature difference and L thickness. Convection is transfer between a fluid and a surface: Q/t = hAΔT, where h is the heat transfer coefficient. Radiation is transfer by electromagnetic waves and matters most in ovens and grills. In a heat exchanger, conduction through the wall and convection on both sides combine.

sections.heading: Thermal and refrigeration calculations
sections.text: For heating a product, Q = m cp ΔT, where m is mass, cp specific heat and ΔT temperature rise. Pasteurisation and sterilisation use a target log reduction. If D is the decimal reduction time, then t = D log(N0/N), with log base 10. Example: reduce a population from 100 000 to 10 per ml, a 4-log reduction. If D at 72°C is 0.5 min, t = 0.5 × 4 = 2.0 min. Sterilisation uses the same equation with a larger target. Refrigeration load is the sum of product cooling, heat through walls, infiltration and internal loads.

sections.heading: Drying and evaporation
sections.text: Drying removes water by evaporation from a wet solid into air. Evaporation removes water by boiling a liquid. Both are mass transfer operations driven by a difference in water vapour pressure. The drying rate depends on air temperature, humidity and velocity, and on the food’s surface and internal resistance. Energy for evaporation is about the latent heat of water, so drying and evaporation are energy-intensive.

keyPoints: Material balance: mass in = mass out + accumulation; at steady state accumulation is zero.
Energy balance: energy in = energy out + accumulation.
Conduction: Q/t = kAΔT/L; convection: Q/t = hAΔT.
Heating duty: Q = m cp ΔT.
At constant temperature, t = D log(N0/N), with log base 10.
Refrigeration load sums product, transmission, infiltration and internal loads; drying and evaporation are mass transfer driven by a water vapour pressure difference.

en.title: Food Rheology and Texture
en.short: Flow behaviour, viscoelasticity and texture profile analysis linked to sensory firmness and chewiness.

sections.heading: Flow and viscosity
sections.text:
Rheology studies how foods deform and flow. Viscosity is resistance to flow: η = τ ÷ γ̇, where τ is shear stress (Pa) and γ̇ is shear rate (s⁻¹), so η is in Pa·s. A Newtonian fluid has constant viscosity; water and oils are close examples. In a non-Newtonian fluid, viscosity changes with shear rate. Shear-thinning foods become thinner when stirred, such as tomato ketchup. Shear-thickening foods become thicker, as concentrated starch suspensions can. A Bingham plastic needs a yield stress before it flows; mayonnaise is modelled this way.

Worked example: if τ = 12 Pa at γ̇ = 30 s⁻¹, η = 12 ÷ 30 = 0.40 Pa·s. At γ̇ = 60 s⁻¹ with τ = 18 Pa, η = 0.30 Pa·s. Viscosity fell, so the sample is shear-thinning.

sections.heading: Viscoelasticity
sections.text:
Many foods are viscoelastic: they show both viscous flow and elastic springback.

Small-amplitude oscillatory tests separate the storage modulus G′ (elastic, energy stored) from the loss modulus G″ (viscous, energy lost). The ratio tan δ = G″ ÷ G′ shows whether the material is more solid-like (tan δ below 1) or more liquid-like (tan δ above 1). Set yoghurt and weak gels often have G′ above G″. Small strains avoid breaking structure.

sections.heading: Texture and sensory links
sections.text:
Texture profile analysis (TPA) compresses a solid food twice, imitating biting. From force-time curves come hardness (peak force), cohesiveness (how well it holds together), springiness (recovery), gumminess = hardness × cohesiveness, and chewiness = gumminess × springiness. Firmness is usually the sensory term for hardness. Chewiness is the sensory effort to chew a food before swallowing. Spreadability is tested by spreading or penetration tests and judged by how easily a paste spreads.

Instrumental values do not automatically equal sensory words. Correlations must be set for each product and panel. A tomato paste may be too firm by penetrometer but still spread easily by hand, so both tests help.

keyPoints: Viscosity η = τ ÷ γ̇, with τ in Pa and γ̇ in s⁻¹, so η is in Pa·s.
Newtonian fluids have constant viscosity; non-Newtonian fluids change viscosity with shear rate.
Viscoelastic foods are described by G′ (elastic) and G″ (viscous), with tan δ = G″ ÷ G′.
TPA gives hardness, cohesiveness and springiness; gumminess = hardness × cohesiveness and chewiness = gumminess × springiness.
Firmness usually corresponds to instrumental hardness, chewiness to chewing effort, and spreadability to ease of spreading.
Instrumental and sensory results must be correlated separately for each food and panel.

en.title: Thermal Processing: Blanching, Pasteurisation and Sterilisation
en.short: Blanching, pasteurisation, canning and UHT, with D, z and F values and how schedules are set.

sections.heading: Blanching and pasteurisation
sections.text:
Blanching is a short heat treatment, about 1 to 5 minutes in hot water or steam at 70 to 100°C, given to fruits and vegetables before freezing or drying. It inactivates enzymes such as peroxidase, expels air and fixes colour. It does not sterilise, so it does not preserve the food on its own.

Pasteurisation kills vegetative pathogens and many spoilage organisms but not spores, so it stays below 100°C. Milk is commonly held at 72°C for 15 seconds. Acid foods (pH below 4.6) can be pasteurised because Clostridium botulinum cannot grow at that pH. Pasteurised food must still be kept cold unless it is acidic.

sections.heading: Sterilisation, canning and UHT
sections.text:
Commercial sterility means destroying all vegetative cells and spores able to grow in the food; a few damaged survivors may remain. Canning seals food in a container and heats it in a retort, a sealed pressure vessel, usually at 115 to 125°C. Low-acid foods (pH above 4.6) need this because C. botulinum spores can germinate in them.

Ultra-high temperature (UHT) treatment heats food to about 135 to 150°C for 2 to 5 seconds, then packs it aseptically into sterile containers. The brief heat preserves more vitamins and flavour than in-container sterilisation.

sections.heading: D, z, F and schedules
sections.text:
Thermal death time (TDT) is the time at a set temperature to kill a stated number of organisms. The D value, or decimal reduction time, is the time at constant temperature to cut numbers by 90%, one log cycle. The z value is the temperature change that alters D tenfold; for C. botulinum spores z is about 10°C. The F value is the equivalent time at a reference temperature, 121.1°C for F0.

Worked example: C. botulinum spores have D121 of about 0.21 minutes. A 12D process gives F0 = 12 × 0.21 = 2.52 minutes, so about 2.5 minutes at 121.1°C is the minimum botulinum cook. With z = 10°C, the same kill at 111.1°C needs 2.52 × 10 = 25.2 minutes.

keyPoints: Blanching inactivates enzymes but does not preserve the food on its own.
Pasteurisation kills vegetative pathogens, not spores, so the product needs refrigeration or acidity.
Commercial sterility is required for low-acid canned foods because C. botulinum spores can grow in them.
D value is the time for a one log (90%) reduction at a fixed temperature.
F0 = D121 × (log N0 − log N); a 12D botulinum cook is the minimum target for low-acid cans.
z is the temperature change that changes D tenfold, about 10°C for C. botulinum spores.

en.title: Non-thermal and Emerging Food Processing Methods
en.short: Refrigeration, freezing, high pressure, pulsed fields, irradiation, ozone, ultrasound and cold plasma.

sections.heading: Cold preservation
sections.text:
Refrigeration holds food near 0 to 4 °C, slowing microbial growth and enzyme action; it does not sterilise. Freezing converts water to ice, stopping growth but not killing all microbes; quality depends on ice crystal size and thawing.

Freeze concentration freezes water, separates the ice, and leaves a concentrate, preserving aroma better than evaporation but losing some solutes. These are established methods; rules on temperatures and cold-chain practice vary by country.

sections.heading: Pressure and pulses
sections.text:
High pressure processing (HPP) uses 100 to 600 MPa to damage microbial membranes and proteins; it is used for ready-to-eat foods and juices, with little heat damage, but spores survive.

Pulsed electric fields (PEF) apply short high-voltage pulses that perforate cell membranes, inactivating microbes in pumpable liquids; particles can protect microbes. Both need validated process controls. Approvals and labelling rules vary by country; check the national regulator.

sections.heading: Irradiation and ozone
sections.text:
Irradiation uses ionising radiation, such as gamma rays, electron beams or X-rays, to break microbial DNA. Dose is measured in gray (Gy). It can control pathogens and insects and inhibit sprouting, but may reduce some vitamins and change flavour at high doses.

Ozone is a strong oxidant that damages cell membranes; it is generated on site for water and produce washing. Both can leave quality changes, and permitted foods, doses and labels vary by country.

sections.heading: Ultrasound and plasma
sections.text:
Ultrasound uses sound waves that create cavitation, tiny bubbles that collapse and produce shear, inactivating some microbes and aiding extraction and emulsification.

Cold plasma is an ionised gas containing reactive species, ultraviolet light and charged particles; it treats surfaces and can inactivate microbes, but may affect colour and lipids. Both are emerging. Their safety must be validated, and regulatory approval varies by country; some uses are not yet permitted.

keyPoints: Refrigeration and freezing slow or stop microbial growth but do not sterilise food.
Freeze concentration removes water as ice and can preserve aroma better than evaporation.
HPP and PEF inactivate microbes without much heating, but spores survive HPP and particles can shield microbes in PEF.
Irradiation dose is measured in gray; it can control pathogens but may change nutrients and flavour.
Ozone, ultrasound and cold plasma are emerging; their safety must be validated before use.
Permitted methods, doses, and labelling rules vary by country, so check the national regulator.

en.title: Preservation Principles and Hurdle Technology
en.short: How aw, pH, salt, sugar, smoke, preservatives and MAP preserve food, and how hurdles combine.

sections.heading: Water activity and pH
sections.text: Water activity (aw) is the water available for microorganisms and chemical reactions, not the total moisture. It is written as a number between 0 and 1. It equals the equilibrium relative humidity divided by 100. Most fresh foods have aw above 0.95. Drying, adding salt or sugar, and freezing lower aw. Acidification lowers pH, usually with organic acids such as lactic, acetic or citric acid. Fermentation produces these acids in situ. Low pH stresses microbial cells and slows enzymes.

sections.heading: Salt, sugar, smoke, chemicals
sections.text: Salt and sugar are humectants: they bind water and lower aw. Salt also draws water out of cells by osmosis. Smoking dries the surface and deposits antimicrobial and antioxidant compounds. Chemical preservatives inhibit specific targets; examples are nitrite in cured meat, sorbate and benzoate in acidic foods, and propionate in bread. Modified atmosphere packaging (MAP) changes the gas around the food to slow spoilage and oxidation.

sections.heading: Hurdle technology
sections.text: Hurdle technology combines several sub-lethal barriers. Each barrier alone is too weak to kill or fully inhibit microorganisms, but together they exhaust repair systems and prevent growth. Because each hurdle can be milder, food keeps better texture, colour and nutrients. A typical fermented sausage uses low pH, reduced aw, salt, nitrite, smoke and vacuum packaging. No single hurdle is enough; the combination is stable.

sections.heading: Worked case
sections.text: A vegetable ferment starts at pH 6.0. Lactic acid bacteria lower it to pH 4.0. Hydrogen ion concentration rises by 10^(6.0 − 4.0) = 100 times. If the product also has 2.5% salt and is packed without oxygen, it has three hurdles. The acid, salt and absence of oxygen each act at a lower level than if used alone.

keyPoints: Water activity is available water, equal to equilibrium relative humidity divided by 100.
Lowering aw, pH or oxygen slows spoilage but may not kill microorganisms.
Salt and sugar lower aw; smoke adds antimicrobial compounds; chemical preservatives target specific organisms.
Modified atmosphere packaging changes the gas around the food to slow spoilage and oxidation.
Hurdle technology uses several sub-lethal barriers so each can be milder.
A pH drop from 6.0 to 4.0 raises hydrogen ion concentration 100-fold (10^2).

en.title: Food Packaging: Materials, Migration and Shelf Life
en.short: Packaging materials, barrier properties, active and intelligent packs, migration and shelf life.

sections.heading: Materials and barriers
sections.text:
Glass is inert and an excellent barrier to gases and moisture, but heavy and fragile. Metal, usually tinplate or aluminium, gives a strong barrier and is light, though acidic foods need an internal lacquer. Paper and board are cheap and printable but have poor barrier properties unless coated or laminated.

Plastics are light, flexible and heat-sealable; polyolefins resist moisture but not oxygen, while PET and EVOH resist oxygen better. A barrier property is a material’s resistance to gases, water vapour, light or aroma. Multilayer laminates combine layers for the needed barrier.

sections.heading: Active and intelligent
sections.text:
Active packaging changes the inside of the pack: oxygen scavengers, moisture absorbers, ethylene absorbers and antimicrobial films. Intelligent packaging senses and signals, such as a time-temperature or freshness indicator.

Modified atmosphere packaging (MAP) replaces air with a gas mix before sealing. Controlled atmosphere (CA) keeps the gas mix constant in a storage room. MAP slows respiration and microbial growth; the mix depends on the food, for example carbon dioxide to slow microbes on meat and fish, and some oxygen for fresh produce.

sections.heading: Migration and shelf life
sections.text:
Migration is the transfer of substances from packaging into food. Food-contact materials must not harm health or change the food unacceptably. EU Framework Regulation (EC) No 1935/2004 sets this rule; plastics face specific migration limits under Regulation (EU) No 10/2011. Nigeria’s NAFDAC regulates food-contact materials.

Tamper evidence is a visible sign of interference, such as a breakable cap or shrink band. Shelf-life testing stores the product under controlled conditions and checks microbial, chemical and sensory quality. If spoilage is twice as fast at 15°C as at 5°C, a 10-day shelf life at 5°C falls to 5 days at 15°C.

sections.heading: Packaging waste
sections.text:
Packaging waste is a large share of municipal solid waste, and recycling depends on local collection. Reduce, reuse and recycle; extended producer responsibility makes producers pay towards collection.

Biodegradable claims need checking, because some materials need industrial composting. No single material is best: the choice balances protection, cost, safety and environmental impact.

keyPoints: Glass and metal give strong gas and moisture barriers; paper needs coating or lamination.
Plastic barrier properties vary, so multilayer laminates combine layers for the needed protection.
Active packaging changes conditions inside the pack; intelligent packaging signals a condition such as time or temperature.
MAP replaces air with a gas mix; CA keeps the gas mix constant in storage.
Migration is packaging-to-food transfer, and food-contact materials are regulated, for example by EU Regulation 1935/2004 and NAFDAC in Nigeria.
Shelf life is confirmed by storage testing, and tamper evidence shows whether a pack has been interfered with.

en.title: Food Fermentation and Starter Cultures
en.short: How lactic acid bacteria, yeasts and moulds ferment foods, and how starter cultures are chosen and handled.

sections.heading: Microbial metabolism
sections.text:
Fermentation is the microbial conversion of sugars and other substrates into acids, gases, alcohols or flavour compounds. Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) are Gram-positive bacteria that make lactic acid. Homofermentative LAB make mainly lactic acid; heterofermentative LAB also make carbon dioxide, ethanol or acetic acid.

Yeasts such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae make ethanol and carbon dioxide. Moulds grow as filaments and release enzymes that break down starch, protein and fat, changing texture and flavour. The acids lower pH and inhibit many spoilage organisms.

sections.heading: Examples in foods
sections.text:
In yoghurt, Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus grow together; acid coagulates milk protein and acetaldehyde gives flavour. Cheese starters such as Lactococcus lactis acidify curd, while Penicillium roqueforti or Penicillium camemberti add blue or surface mould character. Bread yeast makes carbon dioxide that raises dough; sourdough LAB also make lactic and acetic acids.

Ogi, a fermented maize porridge in West Africa, uses LAB and yeasts for acid and aroma. Garri is fermented cassava; LAB acidify it and help reduce cyanogenic compounds. Dawadawa, fermented African locust bean, is an alkaline fermentation driven by Bacillus subtilis, which breaks down protein and gives an ammonia-like flavour.

sections.heading: Starter cultures
sections.text:
A starter culture is a selected preparation of microorganisms added to start and control a fermentation. It may be one strain or a defined mixture. A starter gives more predictable acid, flavour and safety than the natural flora.

Some traditional foods, such as ogi and garri, often ferment spontaneously or by back-slopping, adding part of a previous batch.

sections.heading: Selection and handling
sections.text:
Choose strains that are safe, grow at the process temperature, tolerate salt and acid, and give the wanted flavour without toxins. Handle cultures cleanly: keep frozen or freeze-dried stocks, revive and propagate them in sterile medium, check activity and purity, and avoid repeated back-slopping without checks.

For example, a yoghurt maker using a weak starter may get slow acidification and spoilage; a fresh, active culture and controlled incubation fix it.

keyPoints: Fermentation uses microbes to make acids, gases, alcohols or flavours.
LAB produce lactic acid; homofermentative LAB make mainly lactic acid, while heterofermentative LAB also make gas, ethanol or acetic acid.
Yeasts make ethanol and carbon dioxide; moulds release enzymes that alter texture and flavour.
Yoghurt uses Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus; cheese uses LAB and sometimes moulds; bread uses yeast.
Ogi and garri are LAB-led fermentations; dawadawa is a Bacillus subtilis alkaline fermentation.
Starter cultures should be safe, active and suited to the process, and handled with purity and activity checks.

en.title: Technology of Cereals, Legumes and Oilseeds
en.short: Grain and seed structure, milling, malting, baking, extrusion, oil refining, gari and ogi.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.text: A cereal grain is a caryopsis: the fruit wall is fused to the seed coat. It has bran, endosperm and germ. Bran is the outer layer, including pericarp and aleurone. Endosperm is the starchy store that becomes flour. Germ is the embryo, rich in oil and enzymes. A legume seed has a testa (seed coat), two cotyledons storing starch and protein, and an embryo axis with radicle and plumule. The hilum is the scar.

sections.heading: Milling and malting
sections.text: Dry milling separates grain parts without soaking. Wheat roller milling scrapes bran and germ from endosperm to make flour. Maize dry milling gives grits, meal and flour. Wet milling steeps maize in water with sulphur dioxide, then separates starch, germ, protein and fibre. Cassava starch is also extracted by wet processing. Malting is controlled germination after steeping. Enzymes such as amylases break starch into sugars. Kiln drying stops growth; rootlets are then removed. Malt is used in brewing.

sections.heading: Baking and oils
sections.text: Baking mixes flour, water, yeast and salt. Wheat proteins form gluten, a viscoelastic network. Yeast makes carbon dioxide, expanding the dough. Heat gelatinises starch and sets the gluten; the crust browns by the Maillard reaction. Extrusion forces a moist mix through a die under heat, shear and pressure. Starch gelatinises and protein denatures, giving snacks and breakfast cereals; pasta is extruded cold, then dried. Oilseeds are extracted by pressing or solvent, usually hexane. Refining removes gums by degumming, free fatty acids by neutralisation, colour by bleaching and odours by deodorisation.

sections.heading: Gari and ogi
sections.text: Gari is made by grating cassava, fermenting and pressing it, sieving and roasting the pulp. Roasting, called garification, dries it and develops flavour. Ogi is a fermented maize porridge: maize is steeped, wet milled, sieved and fermented. Fermentation lowers pH and improves flavour. Cassava must be well processed because it contains cyanogenic glycosides. Suppose Amina starts with 100 kg cassava roots and obtains 25 kg gari. Yield = 25 ÷ 100 × 100 = 25%.

keyPoints: Cereal grain has bran, endosperm and germ; legume seed has testa, cotyledons and embryo axis.
Dry milling separates by physical means; wet milling steeps grain and separates starch, protein and fibre.
Malting activates enzymes; baking sets gluten and gelatinised starch; extrusion cooks by heat, shear and pressure.
Oil is extracted by pressing or solvent and refined by degumming, neutralisation, bleaching and deodorisation.
Gari and ogi depend on fermentation and wet processing; cassava must be processed to reduce cyanogenic glycosides.
Yield = product mass ÷ raw mass × 100%.

en.title: Technology of Fruits, Vegetables, Roots and Tubers
en.short: Ripening, senescence, postharvest handling, canning, juicing, drying, freezing, cassava, yam and sweet potato processing

sections.heading: Ripening and senescence
sections.text: Ripening is the controlled set of changes that makes a fruit ready to eat: colour, texture, sugar and aroma change, and respiration and ethylene often rise. Climacteric fruits, such as banana and tomato, ripen with a burst of ethylene; non-climacteric fruits, such as citrus, respond little. Senescence is the later ageing that ends in tissue breakdown. Handling aims to slow ripening and delay senescence without causing chilling injury or decay.

sections.heading: Post-harvest handling
sections.text: Harvest at the right maturity, then cool quickly. Remove field heat, sort out damaged fruit, grade, and store at the correct temperature and humidity. Avoid rough handling because wounds invite mould. Controlled atmosphere and modified atmosphere packaging lower oxygen and raise carbon dioxide to slow respiration. Ethylene can be removed or excluded. Do not store ethylene-producing fruits with sensitive vegetables. Clean water and sanitisers reduce cross-contamination.

sections.heading: Fruit and vegetable processing
sections.text: Canning blanches the food, fills it into cans or jars, seals and heat-sterilises it. Low-acid vegetables need a pressure process to destroy Clostridium botulinum spores; acid fruits need less. Juicing extracts liquid, then pasteurises it; browning is controlled by heat or ascorbic acid. Drying removes water by sun, hot air or freeze-drying. Freezing needs blanching for vegetables, fast freezing for small ice crystals, and steady frozen storage.

sections.heading: Roots and tubers
sections.text: Cassava, yam and sweet potato are starchy staples. Cassava contains cyanogenic glycosides, mainly linamarin and lotaustralin. Peeling removes some; grating, soaking and fermentation let the enzyme linamarase release hydrogen cyanide, which is removed in water or air; drying and cooking drive off more. Garri is grated, fermented, pressed, sieved and roasted. Yam is boiled or dried into flour; sweet potato is cured, stored, or made into flour and chips. Processing methods differ in how much cyanide they remove, so local guidance matters.

keyPoints: Ripening is a controlled softening and sweetening; senescence is later ageing and breakdown.
Ethylene and respiration guide storage; climacteric and non-climacteric fruits differ.
Cooling, grading, correct temperature and humidity, and careful handling extend shelf life.
Canning uses a heat sterilisation step; low-acid foods need a pressure process.
Drying and freezing preserve well when preparation, packaging and storage are correct.
Cassava cyanide is reduced by peeling, soaking, fermentation, pressing, drying and cooking; for high-cyanide cassava, several steps are used together.

en.title: Meat, Fish, Egg and Dairy Technology
en.short: Muscle to meat, chilling, curing, smoking, milk processing, cheese, yoghurt, eggs and fish.

sections.heading: Muscle to meat
sections.text: Muscle is bundles of fibres held by connective tissue. Each fibre contains myofibrils, mainly actin and myosin, and uses glycogen for energy. After slaughter, glycogen becomes lactic acid, pH falls and ATP is used up; the fibres lock in rigor mortis. Later enzymes soften the meat during conditioning. Stress before slaughter can leave meat dark, firm and dry, or pale, soft and exudative.

sections.heading: Chilling, freezing, curing, smoking
sections.text: Chilling slows microbial growth and enzyme action; chilling too fast before rigor can cause cold shortening and tough meat. Freezing stops growth but does not sterilise, and slow freezing makes large ice crystals that damage cells. Curing uses salt, nitrite and sometimes nitrate to lower water activity and develop colour and flavour. Nitrite is controlled because it can form nitrosamines. Smoking dries the surface and deposits preservative phenols. A brine of 20 kg salt in 100 kg water is 20 ÷ 120 × 100 = 16.7% salt.

sections.heading: Milk and dairy
sections.text: Milk is an emulsion of fat in water with proteins, lactose and minerals. Pasteurisation heats it to kill pathogens with minimal change; the exact time and temperature depend on the process and country. Homogenisation forces milk through small valves, breaking fat globules so cream does not separate. Cheese making acidifies or adds rennet to clot casein, then drains whey, salts and ripens the curd. Yoghurt making ferments milk with Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus.

sections.heading: Eggs and fish
sections.text: Eggs are graded, candled and stored cool; washing can remove the protective cuticle and spread bacteria, so practice varies. Fish spoils fast because its muscle has little glycogen, high free amino acids and active enzymes. Chilling in ice, freezing, salting, drying and canning preserve it. Spoilage shows as trimethylamine off-odour, soft flesh and slime. Keep fresh fish near 0 °C and check core temperature.

keyPoints: After slaughter, glycogen falls, pH drops and rigor mortis sets in; conditioning then tenderises meat.
Chilling slows spoilage, while slow freezing makes large ice crystals that damage cells.
Curing uses salt and nitrite to lower water activity and develop colour and flavour; smoking adds phenols.
Brine salt percentage = (salt mass ÷ total mass) × 100; 20 kg salt in 100 kg water gives 16.7%.
Pasteurisation kills milk pathogens, homogenisation stops cream separating, and cheese and yoghurt use clotting or starter cultures.
Eggs are stored cool and handled carefully, while fish spoils fast and needs ice, freezing, salt, drying or canning.

en.title: Technology of Sugar, Confectionery, Beverages and Convenience Foods
en.short: Covers sugar refining, crystallisation, chocolate, candy, fillings, brewing, beverages, tea, coffee, cocoa and snacks.

sections.heading: Sugar refining
sections.text: Raw cane or beet sugar is clarified, decolourised and crystallised. In refining, juice or syrup is treated with lime and heat to remove impurities, filtered, then concentrated under vacuum. Crystallisation is controlled by supersaturation, meaning the syrup holds more sucrose than it can at equilibrium. Seeding gives nuclei, and cooling and evaporation make sucrose crystals grow. Centrifuging separates crystals from molasses. Sugar boiling is the same principle used in candy.

sections.heading: Chocolate and candy
sections.text: Chocolate is a suspension of cocoa solids and sugar in cocoa butter. Cocoa beans are fermented, dried, roasted, shelled and ground; pressing gives cocoa butter and cake. Refining reduces particle size; conching, a long mixing and heating step, removes harsh volatiles. Tempering, controlled heating and cooling, sets cocoa butter crystals so chocolate is glossy and stable. Candy texture depends on sugar concentration and crystallisation. Crystalline candies, such as fondant, have many small crystals; non-crystalline candies, such as toffee, contain interfering agents that stop crystallisation. Bakery fillings balance sugar, fat, starch and water activity (available water) to control texture and microbial growth. Example: to make 10 kg of 20% sugar syrup from 50% syrup and water, use 4 kg syrup and 6 kg water, because 4 × 0.50 = 2 kg sugar and 2 ÷ 10 = 20%.

sections.heading: Beverages
sections.text: Brewing converts malt starch to sugars in mashing (mixing crushed malt with hot water), boils wort (the sugary liquid) with hops, cools it and ferments with yeast. Soft drinks are formulated from water, sugar or sweetener, acid, flavour, colour and preservative, then carbonated. Tea processing withers, rolls, oxidises and dries leaves; green tea skips oxidation. Coffee is processed by dry or wet methods (pulping and fermentation in the wet method), then roasted, ground and brewed. Cocoa is fermented, dried, roasted and ground; pressing separates cocoa butter.

sections.heading: Extruded and convenience foods
sections.text: Extruded snacks are made from starch-rich or protein-rich mixes. Moisture, heat and shear cook the mix in the barrel; pressure release at the die (shaping opening) makes it expand. Drying sets texture. Convenience foods are formulated for shelf life and preparation: freezing, drying, retorting (sealed heating) or chilling, with packaging and water activity controlling quality.

keyPoints: Supersaturation and seeding control sucrose crystal growth in sugar refining.
Chocolate is cocoa solids and sugar suspended in cocoa butter; tempering controls cocoa butter crystals.
Candy texture depends on sugar concentration and on promoting or stopping crystallisation.
Brewing uses mashing, boiling with hops and yeast fermentation; tea, coffee and cocoa have distinct processing steps.
Extrusion cooks by heat and shear and expands the melt at the die.
Syrup blending uses mass balance: sugar before = sugar after, or C1 × M1 = C2 × M2.

en.title: Food Product Development and Formulation
en.short: From idea and screening through formulation, costing, pilot scale-up and launch.

sections.heading: Idea to concept
sections.text:
Product development is a staged process. It starts with a brief: what the product must do, who will buy it and what limits apply. Ideas are screened against consumer need, safety, cost, process fit and the law. A concept is a description or sample tested with users. Stage gates are decision points to continue, change or stop.

A formulation lists ingredients, amounts and process steps. Ingredient functionality is the job each ingredient does, such as water binding, emulsifying, sweetening or giving structure. Choose for function first, then adjust for taste, cost and label claims.

sections.heading: Prototype and reformulation
sections.text: At bench scale, small trials make prototypes. Write the recipe in parts by weight or percentages so it can be repeated and scaled. Change one or a few factors per trial, then use sensory and simple quality tests to guide the next. Reformulation means changing an existing product, for example to cut cost, improve nutrition, remove an additive or meet a new standard. It needs the same checks, because one change can alter texture, safety and shelf life.

sections.heading: Costing
sections.text: Ingredient cost per kilogram is total ingredient cost divided by batch mass. Include yield loss by dividing by saleable mass. Example: a 20 kg batch uses 12 kg base at 500 per kg = 6,000; 5 kg sugar at 400 = 2,000; 2 kg oil at 1,200 = 2,400; 1 kg premix at 3,000 = 3,000. Total = 13,400. Cost per kg = 13,400 ÷ 20 = 670. A 250 g pack holds 0.25 kg, so ingredient cost = 0.25 × 670 = 167.5 currency units. Add packaging, labour, overheads and profit separately.

sections.heading: Scale-up and launch
sections.text: Scale-up moves the recipe to a pilot plant, a small production line. Keep ingredient ratios and critical conditions similar, but expect mixing, heating, filling and losses to differ. Pilot trials measure yield, cycle time and quality. Launch follows production, label and regulatory checks, then monitoring and review.

keyPoints: Product development uses stage gates to screen ideas and decide whether to continue, change or stop.
A formulation states ingredients, amounts and process steps; ingredient functionality is the job each ingredient performs.
Reformulation needs the same safety, sensory and shelf-life checks as a new product.
Ingredient cost per kg = total ingredient cost ÷ batch mass; use saleable mass to allow for yield loss.
In the worked example, 13,400 ÷ 20 = 670 per kg, and a 250 g pack costs 167.5 in ingredients.
Scale-up keeps ratios and critical conditions similar but checks mixing, heating, filling and losses at pilot plant.

en.title: Sensory Evaluation of Food: Tests, Panels and Analysis
en.short: Discriminative, descriptive and affective tests, panel training, triangle and duo-trio tests, hedonic scales, analysis.

sections.heading: Test families
sections.text: Sensory evaluation measures how people perceive food. Discriminative tests ask whether samples differ, not how. Descriptive tests ask trained assessors to rate intensity of named attributes such as sweetness or hardness. Affective tests ask liking or preference, using untrained consumers. The three answer different questions, so choose before designing.

sections.heading: Panels and design
sections.text: Select panelists for sensory acuity, availability and absence of food allergies; descriptive panels need more screening and training than consumer panels. Train descriptive assessors with reference samples and attribute definitions, and check repeatability. Design tests in quiet, odour-free booths with random three-digit codes, balanced order, water or plain crackers between samples, and standard sample size and temperature. Keep sessions short.

sections.heading: Triangle and duo-trio
sections.text: In a triangle test, give three coded samples, two identical and one different, and ask which is odd. The chance of a correct guess is 1/3. In a duo-trio test, give a labelled reference and two coded samples, one matching it, and ask which matches; chance is 1/2. Analyse correct counts with the binomial test: X ~ Binomial(n, p), mean np, variance np(1−p). For 24 triangle assessors with 14 correct, expected = 24 × 1/3 = 8, SD = √(24 × 1/3 × 2/3) = 2.31, z = (14 − 8) ÷ 2.31 = 2.60, significant at 5% one-sided (critical 1.645).

sections.heading: Hedonic tests
sections.text: For liking, use a labelled scale, commonly 9 points from dislike extremely to like extremely. Give each consumer all samples in balanced order and record scores. For two samples use a paired t-test on each person’s difference; for several samples use randomised complete block ANOVA with panelist as block, then post-hoc tests. If ordinal data are not treated as interval, use Friedman or other rank tests. Report means, test statistic, p value and direction of preference.

keyPoints: Discriminative tests detect differences, descriptive tests rate attribute intensity, and affective tests measure liking or preference.
Screen panelists for acuity and availability, and train descriptive assessors with references, but use untrained consumers for hedonic tests.
In a triangle test the chance of a correct guess is p = 1/3; in a duo-trio test it is p = 1/2.
For correct counts use X ~ Binomial(n, p), with mean np and SD √(np(1−p)).
Analyse two-sample hedonic scores with a paired t-test and several samples with randomised complete block ANOVA, using Friedman if ordinal assumptions fail.
Control coding, sample order, temperature and palate cleansing to reduce bias.

en.title: Food Quality Assurance and Management Systems
en.short: Quality terms, specifications, SPC, sampling plans and food quality management systems.

sections.heading: Quality terms
sections.text:
Quality is the degree to which a set of inherent characteristics fulfils requirements. In food it also means fitness for purpose: safe, legal, consistent and acceptable to the buyer.

Quality control (QC) is operational checking of materials and products against limits. Quality assurance (QA) is the planned system that gives confidence that requirements will be met. Total quality management (TQM) is an organisation-wide approach using customer focus, data and continuous improvement.

sections.heading: Specifications and standards
sections.text:
A specification is a written, measurable statement of what a material, process or product must be. It states the characteristic, test method, target and tolerance, sampling and acceptance rule. Limits come from data, law and customer needs.

A standard is an agreed document from a recognised body, or an internal rule, that sets requirements. Codex Alimentarius standards are international food standards; ISO standards are developed by technical committees and reviewed periodically.

sections.heading: SPC and sampling
sections.text:
Statistical process control (SPC) uses control charts to separate common-cause from special-cause variation. An Xbar chart plots sample means. Simplified limits are mean ± 3 standard errors, where standard error = σ ÷ √n. These are not specification limits.

Example: mean 500 g, σ = 5 g, n = 4. Standard error = 5 ÷ √4 = 2.5 g. Limits = 500 ± 3 × 2.5 = 492.5 to 507.5 g. A sample mean of 509 g is above the upper limit, so investigate. An attribute sampling plan gives sample size n and acceptance number c. For n = 50, c = 2, accept if 2 or fewer units fail; reject if 3 or more fail. The operating characteristic curve shows acceptance chance at each quality level.

sections.heading: Management system
sections.text:
A food firm’s quality management system (QMS) is a hierarchy: policy and manual, procedures, work instructions, records. It covers document control, supplier approval, training, calibration, traceability, complaints, audits, corrective action and recall.

ISO 9001 is a quality standard; ISO 22000 combines food safety management with prerequisite programmes and HACCP principles. Certification follows external audit.

keyPoints: Quality is the degree to which characteristics meet requirements; QC checks, QA builds confidence, TQM involves the whole organisation.
A specification states measurable requirements, test method, tolerance, sampling and acceptance rule.
SPC separates common-cause from special-cause variation using control charts.
Simplified Xbar control limits are mean ± 3σ ÷ √n; they are not specification limits.
An attribute sampling plan is defined by sample size n and acceptance number c.
A QMS has policy, manual, procedures, work instructions and records, with audits and corrective action; ISO 9001 and ISO 22000 are common standards.

en.title: HACCP and Food Safety Management Systems
en.short: The seven HACCP principles, the twelve steps, prerequisite programmes and food safety management systems.

sections.heading: HACCP, PRPs and GMP
sections.text: HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point) is a systematic, preventive system that identifies hazards and controls them at points critical to safety. It rests on prerequisite programmes (PRPs): basic hygiene and operational conditions such as cleaning, pest control, training, maintenance, supplier approval and traceability. Good manufacturing practice (GMP) is the part of PRPs covering facilities, personnel, equipment and process controls. HACCP is not a stand-alone plan. It sits inside a food safety management system (FSMS), such as ISO 22000 or a national scheme, which combines PRPs, HACCP and management commitment.

sections.heading: The twelve steps
sections.text: The Codex Alimentarius twelve steps are: 1 assemble the HACCP team; 2 describe the product; 3 identify its intended use; 4 draw the flow diagram; 5 confirm the diagram on site; 6 list hazards, conduct hazard analysis and consider control measures; 7 determine critical control points (CCPs); 8 set critical limits; 9 establish monitoring; 10 establish corrective actions; 11 establish verification; 12 establish documentation and records. Steps 6 to 12 apply the seven principles: hazard analysis; CCP determination; critical limits; monitoring; corrective actions; verification; record keeping.

sections.heading: Principles and a case
sections.text:
A CCP is a step where control is essential and can be monitored. A critical limit is the measurable boundary, such as a temperature or time. Monitoring is scheduled observation or measurement. A corrective action deals with a limit breach and the affected product. Verification checks that the plan works, through audits, calibration and records. Validation provides evidence that controls can achieve safety.

Case: a juice bottler uses metal detection after filling as a CCP. The critical limit is no metal above the detector’s validated test size. Operators monitor with test pieces each shift. If a test fails, they hold product back to the last good check, recheck it and record the action. Verification includes audits and detector checks.

keyPoints: The seven principles are hazard analysis, CCP determination, critical limits, monitoring, corrective actions, verification and record keeping.
The twelve Codex steps prepare the plan in steps 1 to 5 and apply the principles in steps 6 to 12.
Prerequisite programmes and GMP must be in place before a HACCP plan can work.
A CCP is a step where a measurable critical limit is monitored and a breach triggers corrective action.
Verification checks that the plan works; records prove it was followed.
HACCP sits inside a food safety management system and does not by itself guarantee zero risk.

en.title: Food Laws, Standards and Labelling
en.short: Codex, national regulators, standard setting, additives, contaminants, MRLs, claims and label rules.

sections.heading: Who sets the rules
sections.text:
Codex Alimentarius is a joint FAO/WHO commission. It publishes food standards, guidelines and codes of practice. These are not binding, but the WTO SPS Agreement uses Codex as the food-safety reference, so it shapes national law.

Food and drug agencies enforce law: the US FDA, Nigeria’s NAFDAC and India’s FSSAI register or license food businesses, inspect, test, recall and control imports. In the EU, EFSA assesses risk and the Commission manages it. ISO and national bodies issue voluntary technical standards.

sections.heading: How standards are set
sections.text:
A standard is set by risk assessment and risk management. Scientists identify the hazard, study dose-response and estimate exposure. Managers choose a limit that protects health and remains practicable. Drafts go to industry, consumers and governments for comment, then to a committee or commission for adoption.

Additives are allowed only after safety assessment, on a permitted list, with an acceptable daily intake (ADI) and maximum use level. Contaminants have maximum levels; pesticide residues have MRLs.

sections.heading: Additives and contaminants
sections.text:
An additive is added on purpose for a function such as colour or preservation. A contaminant is not added on purpose; it gets in by accident, for example lead or aflatoxin. An MRL is the highest residue legally allowed in or on food, not a target or safety threshold.

Case: a groundnut processor in Kano tests a batch for aflatoxin. If it exceeds the national maximum level, the batch cannot be sold for food; the processor must reject it and find the cause. Limits differ by country; check the official list.

sections.heading: Reading the label
sections.text:
Mandatory label items include food name, ingredients in descending order, allergens, net quantity, date marking, storage instructions, manufacturer name and address, country of origin and lot code. Voluntary items in some countries include nutrition panels, claims, logos and recipes.

Nutrition and health claims are regulated: “low fat” or “high fibre” must meet a defined condition, and health claims need evidence and approval. A “no added sugar” label can still contain natural sugar, so read the nutrition panel. Rules vary by country; check guidance.

keyPoints: Codex Alimentarius is a joint FAO/WHO commission whose standards guide national food law through the WTO SPS Agreement.
National food and drug agencies register or license food businesses, inspect, test, recall and control imports.
A standard is set through risk assessment, risk management, consultation and adoption.
Additives are permitted only after safety assessment, with an ADI and maximum use level.
An MRL is the highest pesticide residue legally allowed, not a direct safety threshold.
Mandatory label items and permitted claims vary by country, so check current regulator guidance.

en.title: Food Safety Risk Assessment and Emerging Hazards
en.short: The four risk assessment steps, risk management and communication, and key emerging food hazards.
